passage:
Class UKG settling-in note. Yogesh, class teacher.
Dhruv (5), week three. He now waves at the gate and says, "Bye Mumma, come at twelve," and walks in alone. Today he spent most of free play building a tall block tower by himself, and only called me over when it fell. At 11:55 he stood at the window watching the gate. When his mother came, he ran to hug her knees for a few seconds, then ran back to show her his tower. Next: I'll tell his mother how well the quick goodbye is working, and keep the same pickup routine.

qa.q: What does Dhruv say at the gate now?
qa.a: "Bye Mumma, come at twelve."

qa.q: Why did Dhruv stand at the window at 11:55?
qa.a: He was expecting his mother and wanted to see her come, trusting she would be back at twelve.

qa.q: Why is keeping the same pickup routine a good plan?
qa.a: A reliable return is what lets Dhruv feel safe enough to play on his own.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother feel when he hugs her knees and then runs back to his tower?
qa.a: She may feel happy and reassured that he has settled and wants to share his school world with her.

grounding: A child settling into school says goodbye, plays alone and checks in briefly at pickup, trusting his mother will return.

passage: At the village school gate, Lakshmi let go of her mother Sangeeta's finger and marched in, tin box swinging. She didn't look back until she reached the neem tree. Then she turned, waved once and ran off to the swing. All morning she played hopscotch with two new friends. When the bell rang, she spotted Sangeeta by the gate, raced over and pressed her face into her sari for a second. Then she tugged her by the hand. "Come, see my chalk house!"

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi turn and wave?
qa.a: At the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi pressing her face into Sangeeta's sari for a second suggest?
qa.a: She was glad and relieved to see her mother, a quick check-in before going back to sharing her day.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta keep doing to help Lakshmi feel brave at school?
qa.a: Being at the gate reliably when the bell rings, so Lakshmi keeps trusting she will come.

qa.q: What is it like for Sangeeta when Lakshmi lets go of her finger without looking back?
qa.a: It may feel proud and a little tender, watching her daughter walk off on her own.

grounding: A young girl leaves her mother at the school gate, plays freely and runs back for a quick check-in at the bell.

passage: Every morning at the kindergarten in Oslo, Lars hung his jacket on the hook with the fox sticker and asked, "Pappa, you come after snack two?" Daniel nodded. "After snack two." Lars hugged him fast and went straight to the sandpit. He dug a river with a new boy, argued about a bucket and made up. When Daniel came through the gate that afternoon, Lars dropped his spade, ran over, hugged his legs hard, then dragged him to the sandpit. "Look, a river! Now go wait there."

qa.q: What sticker is on Lars's hook?
qa.a: A fox sticker.

qa.q: Why does Lars ask "Pappa, you come after snack two?" every morning?
qa.a: Hearing when his father will return helps him feel safe enough to say goodbye and play.

qa.q: What is helpful about Daniel repeating "After snack two"?
qa.a: It gives Lars a clear, reliable promise, so he can trust his father will come back and venture out.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel being told "Now go wait there"?
qa.a: Probably amused and pleased, since it shows Lars feels secure enough to send him off again 😊

grounding: A kindergartner says goodbye, plays independently and runs back for a quick hug at pickup, knowing his father will return.

passage:
At the school gate on his tenth morning, Lalit, five, held out his palm. Papa Saurabh pressed a pretend kiss into it, and Lalit closed his fist and put it in his pocket, their daily ritual. "Pickup at one?" "At one, by the banyan tree." Lalit waved once and ran in without looking back.
In the sandpit he built a long road with a spoon, alone, humming. At one he spotted Papa under the banyan, dashed over, touched his knee and said, "Wait, my road isn't finished." Then he ran back to finish it.

qa.q: Where did Papa say he would be at pickup?
qa.a: By the banyan tree.

qa.q: Why do you think Lalit could run in without looking back?
qa.a: He trusted that Papa would be there at one, and the pocket kiss helped him feel safe enough to go.

qa.q: What makes the pocket-kiss ritual helpful for a child settling in?
qa.a: It gives Lalit a small, reliable goodbye and a promise of return, which makes separating easier.

qa.q: How might Papa Saurabh feel when Lalit touches his knee and runs back to his road?
qa.a: He may feel happy and a little amused that Lalit feels secure enough to check in and go straight back to play.

grounding: A five-year-old settling into school waves goodbye, plays alone and makes a quick check-in at pickup, trusting his father will return.

passage:
I'm Manoj, and I wait at the playschool gate every noon for my granddaughter, so I've watched little Raghav, four, all term. In June he cried and clung to his mother's dupatta. By August he said, "Bye Mumma, see you at twelve," and walked in alone.
I can't know what he feels, but I see him in the play corner driving a toy bus along the wall, talking to it. When the bell goes, he runs to the gate, touches his mother's hand, shows her a paper boat, and then runs back for his bus.

qa.q: What did Raghav drive along the wall in the play corner?
qa.a: A toy bus.

qa.q: What might Raghav's quick touch of his mother's hand suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels safe to explore but still likes to check that his mother, his safe base, is there.

qa.q: How could Raghav's mother support his growing independence?
qa.a: By keeping her twelve o'clock promise every day, so he trusts she will return and keeps venturing out.

qa.q: What might Raghav's mother feel seeing him walk in alone after June's tears?
qa.a: She may feel proud and a little wistful that he needs her less at the gate.

grounding: A grandfather at the gate watches a four-year-old go from clinging to waving goodbye, playing alone and checking in at pickup.
